prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose and poetry that turn memory, the body and dream into an interior cosmology of rare formal ambition and imaginative depth.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged, and I have tried to test it against the round-1 exchange instead of repeating it. On the common criteria, Cărtărescu has the most demonstrable combination of distinctive voice, formal ambition and imaginative depth among the shortlisted writers. As publicly known, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid build memory, the body and dream into a single imaginative architecture, and the poetry belongs to the same project. The chair asked which volumes carry the claim that the late work extends rather than repeats. For me these are the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid, read as one developing undertaking. Evidence of repetition would be recurring set-pieces and images that return without being transformed or complicated, so that length adds volume but not structure. I cannot settle this by direct reading and do not claim to. I have also changed the citation wording. In round 1 I wrote that the work 'remakes the novel on a large scale'. Thin translated coverage of the poetry and essays makes me prefer wording that credits prose and poetry jointly and puts the weight on form and imaginative depth. I would accept a common B047 wording along those lines. The case rests on literary form and sustained quality, not on nationality, symbolism or fame, and not on the number of colleagues who currently agree.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is still evidentiary. I cannot confirm from translations whether the scale of the late books is earned, and Romanian verbal texture reaches me only through translators I cannot verify. The poetry, early prose and essays are thinly covered, so a whole-oeuvre citation leans on the major novels. I also want to avoid treating the translation argument as a verdict on merit. Saying that prose architecture is easier to test in translation than Arabic prosody is a claim about my confidence, not about whether Adonis is the greater writer. Olsson's point that changing the language of a poetic tradition is a different kind of achievement, and not obviously a lesser one, is fair. If original-language readings confirmed the formal claim for Adonis, and the late Cărtărescu volumes proved repetitive on close reading, I would move to B008. Without such readings the two cases are not reliably comparable from where I sit.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first for renewing Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and argument with inherited forms. He says the poems must carry the citation with the essays as support, and that translation uncertainty applies to all poetry and should shape how carefully we read, not how far we trust the candidate. He also says that building a personal cosmos in prose and changing a poetic tradition's language are different achievements, and that the first is not obviously the greater.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and withdraw any implication that a cosmos built in prose outweighs a changed poetic language. My ranking of Adonis second reflects how much I can test, not a lower view of his stature. That answers the chair's question on whether this is evidentiary confidence or merit: it is mainly evidentiary confidence, and expert readings of the Arabic could change it. I agree the poems should carry the citation and the essays should support it. I would also say that the weight of the essays I did not discuss in round 1, so I do not hold a position on it beyond that. Where we still differ is practical. The committee has no original-language reading in hand, and a recommendation has to be made on what it can currently examine.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis first and Cărtărescu fourth. She doubts whether the very long late books justify their scale, says she would move Cărtărescu to first if the quality of the long novels holds, and, in answering my file, says the length of Adonis's career makes timing a pressing question.
responses.response: I take the scale question as the strongest objection to my choice, and I take her stated condition seriously. It is a reasonable test, though I cannot run it by direct reading either. One correction: my round-1 file did not make timing an argument. I wrote that age should decide nothing, and I still hold that. The chair summary records timing only as characterized by her, so I do not want it attributed to my position. On the substance, I accept that if close reading shows the late books are diluted, my case weakens. I disagree that a few overextended volumes would by themselves undo a mature oeuvre, provided the central works hold. That is why I would apply the same test in both directions and not just to Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first on public knowledge and states plainly that she has not read the work directly. She says that if the later volumes only repeat the earlier ones she would move toward Adonis or Anne Carson, and that Adonis's achievement is arguably larger if it can be verified. She also says Wright's case must not lean on cultural significance to make up for a thinner corpus.
responses.response: I share her honesty about the basis of the judgment, and her condition is close to mine. The difference is the alternative I would move to: Adonis, not Carson. Carson's hybrid form is real, but I cannot see how a citation would weigh scholarship and translation against the original poetry, which you also flag. I agree with her point on Wright that the corpus, not the significance of the subject, must carry the case. Her phrase that Adonis is arguably larger if verified is the right way to put it, and I would add that the verification is the whole difficulty.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first and describes Solenoid as a summation that builds on the earlier projects without merely extending them. She ranks Can Xue second, asks whether a consistent method is formula or inexhaustible, and ranks Adonis fifth because the formal claim cannot be verified in translation.
responses.response: Her summation reading is useful but, as she says, it is a claim to test against the text. I framed the late work as extension and she frames it as summation, and neither of us has verified it. If Solenoid does gather and transform the earlier material, that would be strong evidence against repetition. If it only re-stages it, we would be seeing the opposite. I agree with her question about Can Xue and keep her sixth for the same reason, namely uniformity of method over a large output, with the caveat that translated coverage is partial. I also agree that influence on later poets should be kept apart from the lasting force of the poems themselves. That is the point on which my second place for Adonis depends.

uncertainties: Whether the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid, and any later long works, extend the project or merely repeat it. This is unverified and my position depends on it.
How much of Cărtărescu's Romanian verbal texture survives translation, and how thin the translated coverage of his poetry, early prose and essays is for a whole-oeuvre citation.

Whether original-language readings of Adonis would confirm the formal and linguistic claim, and how much the loss of Arabic prosody should discount a poet compared with a prose writer. I cannot resolve this without such readings.
Whether a joint prose-and-poetry citation for B047 is the right scope, or whether the wording should centre on fiction.
For the alternatives: whether Michon's compact corpus supports significance across an oeuvre, and whether Adonis's later collections match the canonical early ones.
No independent source verification is claimed. My knowledge of all candidates rests on general public knowledge and secondary accounts, and not on direct reading of the corpora.
statement.conflict_note: No documented personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer appears in the supplied profile. As noted in the chair summary, my own writing is documentary historical fiction about Central Europe, Nazism and 20th-century trauma, and Cărtărescu belongs to a neighbouring Central and Eastern European tradition. I treat this as context only, not as evidence of preference or merit, and I do not propose recusal. My remarks on the 2025 laureate were given in an official capacity, may reflect a collective position, and are not evidence of my preferences now.
